rationale: Van Hilten and colleagues used wrist activity monitoring in 65 people with idiopathic Parkinson disease and 68 healthy controls. The methods on p. 875 describe exploratory grouping by resting tremor and other motor or sleep variables. These did not change the pattern presented. The investigators found no consistent diurnal fatigue pattern, and the most severely affected groups showed flattened daily motor activity. Rest tremor was a classification variable, and the measured outcomes were general activity and movement indices. The study provides no assigned raw-fig exposure or separate fig effect on rest tremor. All original pages 874–877 were inspected.

Robertson and Hammerstad tested eight patients with Parkinson disease and 11 controls. Tests included voluntary jaw movements, clenching and rhythmic gum chewing. Before versus after usual medication in the patient group, some jaw measures improved and some deteriorated. The exam and discussion distinguish jaw movement deficits from tenderness and pain on palpation. The comparison concerns medication state and jaw kinematics. It provides no dried-date exposure or clinical pain response to dates. All original pages 41–50 were inspected.

Karlsson and colleagues recorded 12 patients with Parkinson disease chewing peanuts before and after levodopa. The same food task was used in both medication states. Opening and closing durations did not clearly change. The occlusal phase shortened, and jaw velocity and vertical displacement increased in the ON state. The food served as a standardized test task. The study has no no-peanut or other food comparator, swallowing-safety assessment, dried-date exposure, or separately graded pain response. All original pages 304–307 were inspected.

The behavioral study separates incremental reinforcement learning from episodic memory in value-based decisions and compares performance in Parkinson disease and controls. Experimental task cues provide no raw-orange intervention or Parkinson fall-frequency response.

The Parkinson study examines turning kinematics across medication states, distinguishing turn strategy and freezing of gait. Falls are discussed as clinical context for turning difficulty. The clinical contrast concerns levodopa and turning. It provides no attributable raw-orange effect on fall frequency.

The case follows blood-pressure dysregulation during evaluation and management of supine hypertension with orthostatic hypotension in Parkinson disease. The original case supplies no raw-orange comparison or exposure-attributable fall-frequency measurement.

The experiment uses fibroblasts from a person with a DNAJB2-related neuropathy and examines heat-shock response and cystamine effects. The measured outcomes are cell-assay variables. No human Parkinson falls or oral raw-orange intervention were studied.

A participant-led n-of-1 study compares effects of deep brain stimulation frequency and uses gait, speech and other observation measures. The treatment variable is stimulation frequency. Neither ground sage intake nor a ground-sage rigidity response is identified.

The clinical-practice article discusses cardiopulmonary exercise testing and the use of measured peak heart rate for exercise prescription in Parkinson disease. The article supplies no ground-sage exposure or comparative rigidity outcome attributable to sage.

This cardiac amyloidosis article describes diagnostic work-up and the complementary use of several imaging approaches. The evaluated condition and investigations provide no dried-date intervention or Parkinson pain estimate.

The published exercise protocol compares a water physical exercise program using high-intensity intervals with its control design in Parkinson disease and specifies trial outcome measures. A protocol for exercise does not establish an exposure-specific clinical pain response to dried dates. The original does not assign dates.

The CALIBRE randomized trial compares carvedilol with variceal band ligation for primary prevention of variceal bleeding in liver cirrhosis. The human treatment groups do not include dried dates, and the paper does not provide a Parkinson pain comparison.

The clinical study compares spatiotemporal gait measures and other outcomes after intramedullary nailing or total hip arthroplasty for unilateral hip fractures in older adults. The comparison is between orthopedic procedures. It supplies no dried-date exposure and no Parkinson pain response attributable to dates.

The Japanese claims study compares persistence and adherence to different levodopa-adjunct medications in older patients with Parkinson disease. The administrative dates and medication outcomes do not supply a dried-date food exposure or pain comparison.

The participant-informed Australian survey follows the patient experience of reaching a Parkinson diagnosis, including respondent-reported pathways and timing. The reported timelines and symptoms provide no intervention with dried dates and no attributable pain estimate.

The case evaluates Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome and cardiac pre-excitation in Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome. The clinical use of Parkinson in the syndrome name does not identify Parkinson disease. The original gives no dried-date or clinical pain comparison relevant to this claim.

The motor functional neurological symptom disorder pilot compares a nocebo-focused cognitive behavioral intervention with controls and reports motor and clinical outcomes. The original reports behavioral treatment for a different disorder. It has no dried-date exposure and no Parkinson-specific pain outcome.

The 12-month ecopipam report follows pediatric participants with Tourette syndrome and evaluates safety and clinical effects. The study's time entries and medication outcomes supply no dried-date or Parkinson pain experiment.

The SmarTKRing protocol tests physiotherapy with wearable activity monitoring after total knee replacement. It defines postoperative follow-up and outcome measures. This protocol does not report a dried-date intervention or a pain effect attributable to food in Parkinson disease.

The case documents endovascular verapamil administration and monitoring for vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage. The procedural narrative provides no dried-date exposure or Parkinson pain comparison.

The early-phase Parkinson study evaluates safety of an investigational GDNF gene therapy and reports clinical follow-up. The intervention and adverse-event assessments do not supply a dried-date intervention or a Parkinson pain response to dates.

The REONPARK interim report describes COMT-inhibitor use with levodopa in people with early Parkinson motor fluctuations. Its medication comparison and clinical assessments do not assign dried dates or independently measure their effect on pain.

The SMELL randomized protocol compares approaches to training persistent post-COVID olfactory impairment and specifies olfactory follow-up. The study concerns postviral smell impairment and does not provide a dried-date or Parkinson pain outcome.

The original randomized mechanistic trial compares minocycline with placebo for chronic low back pain, including imaging markers of inflammation. The exposure is an antibiotic and the clinical condition is chronic low back pain. It provides no dried-date effect on Parkinson pain.

The study measures a serum alpha-synuclein fragment associated with calpain-1 cleavage to distinguish groups including Parkinson disease. Biomarker differences provide no measured raw-fig intervention or raw-fig effect on rest tremor.

The phase I/II trial reports safety and clinical motor outcomes after an investigational dopaminergic cell therapy for Parkinson disease. The reference to figures concerns study illustrations. The trial supplies no oral raw-fig exposure or fig-specific rest-tremor result.

The report describes levodopa-responsive parkinsonism in spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 and discusses the clinical and genetic diagnosis. The case supplies no oral raw-fig comparison and no rest-tremor effect attributable to fruit.

The physiology study compares neural responses to paired deep brain stimuli and records evoked activity in basal ganglia targets. The measured effects are stimulation responses. The original has no raw-fig intake or fig-attributable clinical rest tremor comparison.

The case follows clinical motor changes after a stroke in primary familial brain calcification and interprets the lesion in relation to thalamic targets. Clinical changes after a lesion cannot establish a dietary raw-fig effect on Parkinson rest tremor. The original assigns no fig exposure.

The study compares smartphone measurements of voice, finger tapping and gait for identifying early Parkinson disease. Its movement measurements and classifiers do not provide a raw-fig intervention or an ingredient-specific rest-tremor outcome.

The retrospective imaging study uses baseline dopamine transporter PET to predict onset of levodopa-induced dyskinesia. Dyskinesia prediction and figure labels supply no oral raw-fig or Parkinson rest-tremor response.

The original develops predictors of incident dementia in Parkinson disease and assesses prognosis using clinical measures. A dementia prediction study supplies no assigned raw-fig exposure or separate rest-tremor response to fig.

The study compares Parkinson-related immune phenotypes and alpha-synuclein-reactive T cell populations. The original immune assays do not provide an edible raw-fig exposure or dietary rest-tremor response.

The clinical report evaluates a Roy Adaptation Model nursing intervention with quality of life and psychological and social outcomes in Parkinson disease. The program and clinical measures supply no isolatable raw-fig intervention or fig effect on rest tremor.

The case series evaluates patellar reflex before and after an acupuncture protocol in people with Parkinson disease. A reflex response after acupuncture is a different comparison and endpoint from Parkinson rest tremor after raw fig consumption.

The report characterizes progressive generalized dystonia within an NBEA-related neurodevelopmental presentation. The diagnostic case supplies no dried-date exposure, idiopathic Parkinson apathy comparison, or food response.

The study surveys artistic and everyday creativity and perceived changes in people with Parkinson disease. Self-reported creativity and recorded history provide no dried-date exposure or independently attributed apathy response.

The PPMI cohort study identifies memory-predominant and visuospatial-predominant profiles among 75 participants with Parkinson disease dementia. Table 2 reports apathy in 23 of 50 and 14 of 25, respectively, with p = 0.469. The apathy values describe groups defined by cognitive profiles. The authors do not compare dried-date exposure or a date-induced apathy change.

The structural MRI analysis examines cognition and impulse control disorders in a Parkinson cohort, with other neuropsychiatric factors discussed. The reported variables supply no oral dried-date comparison or independently measured change in Parkinson apathy attributable to dates.
